newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - U.S. to seek revenge on Bunds in 1997.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - U.S. to seek revenge on Bunds in 1997.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries got off to a sour start this year but analysts and investors said on Thursday they would prove a better bet in 1997 than an overpriced Bund market.

In the short run T-notes' yield premium over Bunds could widen further as Treasuries suffered from the view the U.S. economy was expanding too briskly. But by year-end, worries about European monetary union and Bund supply were expected to push German yields much higher, possibly above U.S. levels.
"We're getting the classic trend of U.S. underperformance in a bearish market," said Phyllis Reed of BZW in London.

"That was a big trend last year," said Reed, European bond strategist at the British bank. "This year the trend will break down and you will see Europe underperforming despite the fact that we don't have a bullish outlook on U.S. bonds."

The gap between U.S. 10-year yields over Bunds was at 63 basis points at 1307 GMT. In 1996, Treasuries started the year with a 60 basis point yield discount to Bunds. Then, as signs of U.S. economic strength began to pour in, the situation reversed and by April German yields had dipped below those of the U.S.
But this year Treasuries will outmuscle Bunds, even as both markets deteriorate, because the German economy will perk up at the same time the U.S. slows, analysts said.

"In the short term, both markets in our view have a negative bias," said Graham McDevitt, senior analyst at Paribas Capital Markets in London. "Once the spread gets back out to that 70-75, on a longer term basis we're telling people to switch out of core Europe and into the U.S.

McDevitt said that if the U.S. Federal Reserve decided to raise interest rates, the U.S. economic slowdown would be even Paul Meader, managing director at Rothschild Bank Switzerland in Guernsey, also said cyclical factors would favour the U.S. debt market.
"The economic cycle is now swinging towards favouring U.S. bonds over those in Europe, particularly those in Germany."
Meader and BZW's Reed both said Treasuries would gain a relative advantage over German debt because of the ramifications of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

In 1996, European convergence sped up as high-yielding bonds outperformed Bunds even as German yields declined. But Reed said in 1997 German yields were likely to move higher towards the levels in peripheral bond markets.

She said the mark was already suffering in late 1996 as investors contemplated the effects of EMU, but that weakness had not yet filtered into Bunds. Reed saw the 10-year German yield rising to around 6.75 by year-end from 5.89 percent currently.
"We see Bund yields rising back above the U.S. by the end of the year to 25 over," she said.
Meader too said the U.S./German yield differential would be eroded during the course of the year, although he said there may still be scope for peripheral European markets to fare better.

Another reason for Reed's bearish outlook on Germany was the weight of supply in the next couple of years. Reed cited official data showing around 150 billion marks of redemptions coming up in 1997 and a similarly high amount in 1998.
"Some of this bond issuance is reunification debt expiring. We know that reunification was pretty much financed by oversees investors," Reed said.

These investors, she added, were less likely to buy back into German debt given the historically low level of yields and growing worries about the status of the new euro currency, in which such debt would be repaid.
